text.p: Italy Sunday named a new chairman to oversee asset sales at IRI and start winding up operations at the giant state-owned company that dictator Benito Mussolini set up in 1933 to rescue Italian banking.

The Treasury said the new appointments, which would see outgoing chairman Michele Tedeschi replaced by Gian Maria Gros-Pietro, would be put to an IRI shareholders' meeting on Monday. The Treasury is sole shareholder.
The widely expected move came after Tedeschi, IRI chairman since 1994, rejected criticism of his lukewarm stance on the sale of state-owned assets at the troubled company.

"The mandate that we intend to give the new board is to carry forward the privatisations and liquidations of companies which come under IRI with a commitment to conclude the process and proceed to the cessation of the institute's activities within three years," the statement said.
It thanked Tedeschi for what the Treasury called the dedication and expertise "with which he has led the institute in its difficult phase of transition."

Gros-Pietro, an economist, is a board member of ANAS, the national road maintenance company, and since 1994 has been a member of the Treasury's privatisation committee. He is also a close acquaintance of Prime Minister Romano Prodi, a former IRI chairman.

IRI, established by Mussolini to rescue the Italian banking industry, had debts of 23.5 trillion lire ($14 billion) last year. Government eagerness for a quick sell-off of assets has led to tensions with the outgoing board.

Prodi was twice chairman of IRI, from 1982-89 and from 1993-94, before resigning to be replaced by Tedeschi. Prodi then entered the political arena culminating in his victory in April 1996 elections at the head of a centre-left government.
The largest industrial group in the country, the sprawling giant controls hundreds of businesses in sectors as diverse as broadcasting and shipbuilding.

Italian newspapers have reported that Treasury plans foresee IRI not being assigned new tasks but concentrating of privatising existing assets, starting with highway maintenance company Autostrade and Rome airports.
Other assets owned by IRI include engineering group Finmeccanica, shipbuilder Fincantieri and state airline Alitalia.
In 1993 IRI privatised its Credito Italiano and Banca Commerciale Italiana banks and its SME food business. In 1996, IRI sold off its remaining ILVA steel interests.
